questions.question: Which statement best describes a singularity of a function $f$ at $x_0$?
options: $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ but discontinuous at every nearby point.
$f$ fails at $x_0$ but is regular in a punctured neighbourhood.
$f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ but not continuous nearby.
$f$ is undefined on every interval containing $x_0$.
questions.explanation: A singularity at x_0 means f fails to be defined or continuous at x_0, while being defined and continuous in a punctured neighbourhood of x_0.
questions.source_support: Definition of singularity and punctured neighbourhood.

option_explanations: Being continuous at x_0 but discontinuous nearby is the opposite of a singularity.
Being differentiable at x_0 implies continuity, so it is not a singularity.
Being undefined on every interval is too broad; a singularity is isolated.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: Why is a punctured neighbourhood used when identifying a singularity at $x_0$?
options: It requires $f$ to be undefined at every point near $x_0$.
It checks that $f$ is well behaved near $x_0$ except possibly at $x_0$ itself.
It replaces the need to know whether $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.
It means that $x_0$ must be an endpoint of the domain.
questions.explanation: A punctured neighbourhood is used to check that f is well behaved near x_0 (except possibly at x_0 itself), isolating the singularity.
questions.source_support: Definition says $f$ is defined and continuous in a punctured neighbourhood of $x_0$.

option_explanations: The punctured neighbourhood checks regularity near x_0, not undefinedness.
Whether f is continuous at x_0 is relevant (a singularity means it fails there).
A punctured neighbourhood surrounds $x_0$ on both sides, so $x_0$ is an interior point, not an endpoint; e.g. $(-1,1)\setminus\{0\}$ is a punctured neighbourhood of $x_0=0$.
